title: 2026-06-12-tech-deep-dive-multi-region-routing-failover
summary: Redwood SEs walked HorizonPay through a proposed multi-region routing and failover architecture. Focus areas: policy routing (latency vs cost vs data residency), regional capacity and warm pools, DR playbooks for zone/region failures, KV cache shard and prefix caching implications for failover, batching impacts on tail latency, and quantization/model-variant fallbacks. Agreed next steps: run cross-region benchmarks, share routing policy templates, provide example DR playbooks and KV cache invalidation strategies, and schedule a follow-up POC kickoff.
action_items: Maya Liu: Share routing policy template and sample config (due 2026-06-16)
Carlos Mendez: Run synthetic cross-region latency-throughput benchmarks with HorizonPay sample prompt set (due 2026-06-19)

Samir Patel: Provide representative prompt/seq-length distribution and golden outputs for quality checks (due 2026-06-18)

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-06-12 16:00 UTC, Duration: ~62 minutes. Attendees: Maya Liu (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (HorizonPay CTO), Ben Lee (Infra), Samir Patel (ML).

[00:00] Maya Liu: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — multi-region routing, failover playbooks, and some of the runtime tradeoffs around KV cache, batching, and quantization. Carlos will lead on the technical side.

[00:22] Carlos Mendez: Hi. Cool, so at a high level we think about routing policies along three axes: latency, cost, and data residency. You can prioritize one or write a policy that scores requests. For example, read-only queries from EU users should prefer eu-west, fallback to us-west if capacity or region fail.

[00:45] Priya Sharma: Yeah, our main ask is: low tail latency for payment flows in EU and APAC, and strict data residency for logs. We want to avoid egress where possible. How would Redwood handle that?

[01:10] Carlos Mendez: You can pin routes by region with policy rules: region_preference -> allowed_regions -> fallback_strategy. Fallbacks can be tiered — e.g., first try dedicated eu pool, then shared eu hosts, then us-west. We also support model-variant fallbacks if a quantized variant is compatible.

[01:38] Ben Lee: Quick Q — when you fail over to another region, what happens to the KV cache? We rely heavily on prefix caching to speed up long conversations. If the cache is warm in eu-west but then failover to us-west occurs, do we see cold cache penalties?

[02:05] Carlos Mendez: Good question. KV cache is local to the serving node; we don't replicate hot token KV across regions in the hosted offering by default because of consistency and egress cost. Our recommended pattern: maintain short TTL prefix caches at the edge and rely on request-level routing to favor warm regions. For cross-region failover, expect cache cold-start which increases token compute/time until the KV warms.

[02:33] Samir Patel: That cold-start could be problematic for our sub-200ms SLAs. Any mitigations?

[02:46] Carlos Mendez: A few options — one is proactive warm pools: keep minimal warm sessions across regions for critical customers. For latency-sensitive flows, we suggest a small dedicated warm pool in each target region with periodic keep-alive prompts to preserve KV. Another is prefix snapshotting — we can snapshot KV prefixes and load them on failover, but that requires custom integration and has consistency tradeoffs.

[03:20] Priya Sharma: Snapshotting seems heavy. How about just routing policy that never crosses regions for certain flows?

[03:30] Maya Liu: Exactly — you can tag traffic by flow type. Payments chat flows go eu-only with strict fallback to an in-region standby only. If that in-region standby is down, the policy can either queue requests or send to an emergency region with an explicit SLA degradation notice.

[03:52] Ben Lee: Ok, how do we express the queueing behavior? We have spikes and can't lose requests.

[04:05] Carlos Mendez: We expose a route action: immediate_reject | queue_with_backoff | failover. Queueing is at the request router layer for short windows (seconds to low minutes) and relies on upstream client retries. For longer doors you need durable queues (like SQS) in front of the API.

[04:34] Priya Sharma: What about autoscaling and warm pool sizes? We need help sizing based on our expected qps across three regions.

[04:48] Carlos Mendez: We'll work from the QPS and  P95 latency targets. As a rule of thumb, for conversational workloads with kv-heavy long seqs, plan for lower concurrency per GPU due to KV cache and memory. For example, Llama-like models at 8k context have throughput X — (note: transcription may garble some numbers here) — but we can supply a spreadsheet. Warm pool guidelines: small base + autoscale ramp with pre-warming thresholds.

[05:20] Samir Patel: Can you share that spreadsheet? Also we use quantized 4-bit in prod for cost. If we fail over to another region, do you automatically use the same quantized model variant?

[05:36] Carlos Mendez: We try to match model variants, but if the exact quantized binary isn't available in the fallback region we can route to a compatible variant — might be different quantization or slightly different kernel that trades cost for latency. We highly recommend keeping identical model artifacts in all critical regions to avoid quality/latency delta.

[05:58] Ben Lee: Is there a significant perf delta between regions if the hardware differs? E.g., G5 vs A2?

[06:12] Carlos Mendez: Yes — kernel selection matters. We pick kernels based on architecture. Different GPUs lead to different per-token latency and throughput. Policy routing can include hardware_preference list so you can prefer regions with X hardware for heavy workloads.

[06:30] Maya Liu: Another layer is cost-aware routing — you might prefer a cheaper region for non-critical embeddings, but enforce strict region for PII-related calls.

[06:45] Priya Sharma: On security — we need to know about KMS and audit trails when failing over. If we route a request to us-west, does key material ever leave eu-west?

[07:00] Carlos Mendez: No — with Private deployments you control KMS. For hosted, we support customer-managed keys in region to avoid cross-region key egress. Audit logs record routing decisions and region used. We'll send security docs, but rule of thumb: if keys are region-restricted, failover to a region with the key or use a policy that disallows cross-region decrypt.

[07:30] Ben Lee: What about SSO and RBAC across regions for console ops?

[07:38] Maya Liu: Console is global but RBAC and SSO bridge to your IdP. For Private, you run the control plane in your VPC and we can keep the control plane region-bound as requested.

[07:50] Priya Sharma: Let's talk DR playbooks. If an entire region goes down, what's the recommended runbook?

[08:02] Carlos Mendez: Our suggested DR playbook steps (high level): 1) Detect and categorize incident (region outage vs degraded performance) 2) Switch routing to standby regions per policy, 3) Enable emergency warm pools, 4) If KV consistency required, accept degraded latency and kick off KV rehydration, 5) Post-incident reconciliation and metrics. We'll provide a template playbook.

[08:28] Samir Patel: Regarding KV rehydration — how do we reconcile stateful session continuity? Sessions are important for our multi-step auth flows.

[08:40] Carlos Mendez: You have options: sticky sessions (keep route to original region until recovery), session replication (custom integration to store KV snapshots in cross-region durable store), or accept stateless recovery with a short lived token approach. Each has tradeoffs. Sticky maintains latency but reduces failover resilience; replication is complex but gives continuity.

[09:06] Ben Lee: Any guidance for the snapshot frequency and size? Our average session KV is ~1MB but can spike.

[09:19] Carlos Mendez: For 1MB snapshots at scale, network and storage cost grows quickly. Usually we only snapshot essential prefixes (auth tokens, short-term context). Keep snapshots incremental and compressed. We'll add an example with estimated costs.

[09:40] Maya Liu: Also remember batching behavior — batching increases throughput but can worsen tail latency during failover. If you use aggressive batching, cold cache penalties might be amplified.

[09:55] Samir Patel: We currently batch requests in 50ms windows to improve cost. Does Redwood support dynamic batching policies by route?

[10:05] Carlos Mendez: Yes — batching is per-route configurable with target_latency_window. For critical low-latency routes, we recommend small or no batching. For embeddings or background tasks, larger windows improve efficiency. During failovers you might switch to lower batching to avoid additional queuing.

[10:28] Priya Sharma: How do we handle quality regressions if a fallback model variant is slightly different? We can't have payment flows giving inconsistent answers.

[10:40] Carlos Mendez: Two mitigations — first, use model pinning for critical flows so fallback won't touch the model family. Second, synchronous checks: when a fallback triggers, run a lightweight verification against golden outputs we store; if unacceptable, trigger custom routing (e.g., hold requests, escalate). We also support A/B rollback and can route a small percentage to fallback for real-time monitoring.

[11:08] Ben Lee: Are there built-in alerts when a routing fallback occurs?

[11:15] Maya Liu: Yes, we stream routing events into the console and support webhooks. You can get alerts for failover count, percent of traffic rerouted, and increases in p95.

[11:28] Priya Sharma: Let's talk numbers — what percent p95 increase should we expect on cold KV after cross-region failover?

[11:38] Carlos Mendez: Depends on model and context length. For long-context models, cold KV can add tens to a few hundreds ms per token on the first few tokens while cache warms. End-to-end p95 could jump from 150ms to 400-700ms for initial requests, then settle. We should run a benchmark with your sample prompts to quantify.

[12:02] Samir Patel: Ok please run that benchmark. Also, do you support pre-warming sequences automatically?

[12:12] Carlos Mendez: We have a pre-warm API; you can provide representative sequences to keep KV warm. This works well for a small set of high-value sessions.

[12:23] Ben Lee: For VPC/private — if we host on-prem, do the same routing primitives exist? We want identical behavior between hosted and private.

[12:35] Carlos Mendez: Yes, the control plane is similar; for Private we provide the same policy language with local routing decisions. Some hosted-only features (like multi-tenant shared pools) behave differently, but core routing/fallback primitives are available.

[12:52] Priya Sharma: About compliance — we need audit trails for every routing decision and who triggered overrides. Is that available?

[12:59] Maya Liu: Audit logs include routing decisions and operator actions. For Private, logs stay in your VPC. For hosted, we can provide log export to your log store.

[13:12] Carlos Mendez: Another caveat — when you rely on third-party CDNs or edge-network routing, the client source IP may not reflect true origin, which complicates geo-routing. For those cases, we recommend embedding region hints in request headers from your edge.

[13:35] Samir Patel: Noted.

[13:40] Priya Sharma: Can you provide example routing policies? We'd like to see one that enforces EU-only for PII, another that is cost-prioritized for embeddings, and a strict low-latency one for auth flows.

[13:52] Maya Liu: We'll attach three template policies after the call.

[14:00] Ben Lee: Regarding bench runs, we need to know the exact config used — model file names, quantization bits, GPU types, batch windows.

[14:10] Carlos Mendez: We'll include full config. For quantization, note that some 4-bit kernels are hardware-specific so perf can vary. We'll include kernel and binary names.

[14:22] Priya Sharma: How do rollouts look in a cross-region scenario? If we push a model that behaves worse in one region, can we canary by region?

[14:35] Carlos Mendez: Yes — rollouts can be scoped by region, model, and route. You can do canary percentages per region and auto-rollback based on quality signals (golden prompt evals) and infra signals (error rate, p95).

[14:52] Samir Patel: Any gotchas for logs and observability during failover? We want traces to show originating region and final serving region.

[15:02] Maya Liu: We include request-level metadata: origin_hint, routed_region, served_by_instance, and model_variant. That should satisfy end-to-end tracing.

[15:15] Priya Sharma: Great. A few quick operational questions: 1) How long does a warm pool scale-up take? 2) Can we reserve capacity across regions?

[15:25] Carlos Mendez: Warm pool scale-up is minutes with pre-warm hooks; if you need sub-minute, you need hot standby. Reserved capacity is supported via Dedicated and Private — you can reserve per-region pools.

[15:40] Ben Lee: For reserved pools, can we mix hardware types? We might want a mix of higher perf for auth and lower cost for background tasks.

[15:49] Carlos Mendez: Yes, pools are tagged by hardware and routing policies can prefer specific tags.

[16:00] Priya Sharma: Anything else we should be aware of when designing our DR playbook?

[16:06] Carlos Mendez: One more: test failovers regularly. Automated DR drills that exercise failover paths for short windows reveal sticky-session issues and snapshot gaps. Also ensure your monitoring alerts are tuned to detect gradual capacity degradation, not just full outage.

[16:26] Maya Liu: Let's recap next steps (quick): Redwood will share routing policy templates, DR playbook draft, benchmarking configs, and a recommended warm pool sizing spreadsheet. HorizonPay will provide qps by region, sample prompts, and security contacts. SE will run cross-region benchmarks and demo pre-warm API.

[16:48] Priya Sharma: That works. Any blockers on your side?

[16:52] Maya Liu: None. We'll aim to share the materials by mid next week.

[16:58] Ben Lee: Thanks everyone.

[17:01] Carlos Mendez: Thanks, we'll follow up with links.

[17:05] [end] Note: transcript has occasional minor transcription errors and run-on lines typical of Fireflies exports.
